title: Understanding Merge History
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and boundaries of understanding merge history.
Choose and interpret a Git command relevant to understanding merge history using a disposable repository.

content.intro: This lesson introduces understanding merge history as part of Merging and Resolving Conflicts. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: A merge commit records multiple parents, preserving the ancestry of the merged histories. First-parent views simplify one branch’s integration story but omit some details from the full graph.

content_blocks.title: Branches are references to commits
content_blocks.alt_text: Two branch names can point to different commit tips while sharing earlier history. The branch name moves when new commits are created.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** A merge commit records multiple parents, preserving the ancestry of the merged histories. First-parent views simplify one branch’s integration story but omit some details from the full graph.

For **Understanding Merge History**, keep the named subtopics in view: Parent commits; Merge commit ancestry; First-parent history; How merges affect later comparisons. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Merge commits can have multiple parents. Graph shape helps explain ancestry but does not replace reviewing the merged patch.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

task: Create or use two clearly named branches in a disposable repository. Make one small change on each, inspect the commit graph, perform the relevant integration step, then verify the final files and history.
hints: Use a read-only inspection command before any operation that changes files, refs or remote state.
After the example, verify with git status --short --branch and/or git log --oneline --graph as appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
